title:
Interface-Engineered
Hafnia–MoS2 Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistors
Enabling a Nearly Ideal Memory
Window with Back-End-of-Line Compatibility
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0
abstract:
Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, with their atomically
thin
geometry and excellent electrostatic control, are promising channel
materials for ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs). However,
integrating high-quality ferroelectric gate stacks onto these ultrathin
channels in a manner compatible with modern semiconductor manufacturing,
particularly under back-end-of-line (BEOL) constraints, remains a
major challenge primarily due to interfacial instability. Here, we
demonstrate interface-engineered top-gated 2D FeFETs based on monolayer
molybdenum disulfide (MoS_(2)) integrated with ferroelectric
hafnium–zirconium oxide (HZO) via atomic layer deposition.
An ultrathin high-κ yttrium oxide (Y_(2)O_(3)) interfacial layer serves as both a nucleation and protection layer,
enabling conformal HZO growth while preserving a sharp van der Waals
interface. All fabrication steps were conducted below 300 °C,
fully satisfying BEOL thermal budgets. The resulting devices exhibit
intrinsic polarization-driven switching rather than trap-dominant
behavior. Notably, they achieve a nearly ideal memory window of 3.6
V, corresponding to ∼90% of the theoretical maximum, under
a low operating voltage of ±3.5 V, along with distinguishable
nonvolatile switching characteristics. These results establish a CMOS
and BEOL-compatible interface engineering strategy for integrating
high-performance 2D FeFETs, providing a scalable pathway toward monolithic
3D systems for future embedded memory and logic-in-memory applications.

content.text:
The exponential growth of data-centric
and edge computing has exposed the energy and latency bottlenecks
of conventional semiconductor devices and computing architectures.
As a result, there is an increasing demand for next-generation device
solutions that simultaneously offer low power consumption, fast switching
speed, and integrated memory–logic functionality.
−



 Ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) have emerged as
promising candidates by combining nonvolatility, ultrafast switching,
and a compact one-transistor (1T) footprint, making them ideally suited
for embedded memory and in-memory computing.
−

 Among various
FeFET platforms, hafnium–zirconium oxide (HZO)-based FeFETs
have attracted particular attention due to their robust ferroelectricity
at nanometer-scale thicknesses, scalability to advanced nodes, and
seamless compatibility with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor
(CMOS) processes.
,−


 To enable their deployment in
system-level architectures, particularly monolithic three-dimensional
(M3D) integration, it is essential that both the ferroelectric and
channel layers be fabricated under back-end-of-line (BEOL) constraints
below 400 °C without compromising interface quality.
,−

In this context, two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, especially
transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), have emerged as highly promising
BEOL-compatible channel materials. In addition to recent reports of
sub-400 °C synthesis, their atomically thin bodies provide excellent
electrostatic gate control and maximize gate efficiency.
−


 Furthermore, ultrathin geometry helps suppress depolarization fields,
which is critical for stabilizing ferroelectric polarization in ultrascaled
devices. The absence of dangling bonds also yields chemically inert
surfaces, suppressing interfacial reactions, minimizing charge traps,
and preventing parasitic oxide formation (e.g., native SiO_(2) in silicon-based systems). These attributes collectively enable
low-voltage operation, large memory windows, and improved reliability
in FeFETs.
−

Despite these advantages, the realization of CMOS-compatible
2D
FeFETs and the integration of high-quality ferroelectric gate stacks
onto atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) channels under BEOL-compatible
conditions remain major challenges, particularly for top-gated architectures.
−


 The chemically inert nature of vdW surfaces significantly hinders
uniform nucleation during atomic layer deposition (ALD). While recent
advances in 2D MOSFETs have demonstrated that this limitation can
be partially overcome by introducing seed layers, 2D FeFETs with top
HZO gate stacks impose stricter requirements.
,−

 Specifically, the seed layer must be ultrathin and
possess a high dielectric constant to ensure efficient gate coupling
while minimizing interfacial traps. Moreover, unlike nonferroelectric
dielectrics, ferroelectric HZO typically requires postdeposition crystallization,
typically achieved by rapid thermal annealing, to stabilize the orthorhombic
phase responsible for polarization switching. Such high-temperature processes, however, can degrade the structural
and electrical properties of 2D channels, leading to interfacial damage
and defect formation. These interfacial defect states often induce
trap-dominated switching, rather than intrinsic ferroelectric-driven
switching, ultimately reducing the memory window and degrading the
overall device reliability. Consequently, most prior demonstrations
of 2D FeFETs have relied on back-gated architectures or metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor
(MFMIS) capacitive stacks, which are inherently less scalable and
unsuitable for practical system-level integration.
,,,,

In this work, we demonstrate a monolayer MoS_(2) FeFET
with a top-gated architecture, fabricated entirely under BEOL-compatible
conditions (<300 °C) using an ultrathin high-κ yttrium
oxide (Y_(2)O_(3)) interfacial layer and annealing-free
HZO. This integration strategy enables conformal ALD growth while
preserving a well-defined vdW interface. The fabricated FeFETs exhibit
intrinsic polarization-dominated switching with a large memory window
(3.6 V at gate voltage sweep of ±3.5 V), nonvolatile characteristics,
and state-of-the-art normalized memory performance among BEOL-compatible
2D FeFETs. These results represent a key advance toward scalable,
low-power, and CMOS-compatible FeFETs.
Results and Discussion

Design of a Monolayer MoS_(2) FeFET with a Top HZO Gate
Stack

To realize a high-performance, HZO-top-gated FeFET
with an atomically thin MoS_(2) channel, it is essential to
achieve conformal deposition of ferroelectric HZO onto the MoS_(2) surface, while preserving the pristine vdW interface and
minimizing interface trap formation. To this end, an ultrathin high-κ
Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer is introduced, serving
both as a seed layer for HZO growth and as a protection layer for
the 2D channel during ALD (a). The effective dielectric constant of the Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer is estimated to be approximately
12.6 from separate capacitance measurements of metal–insulator–metal
(MIM) capacitors (Figure S1). Equally important
is the stabilization of the orthorhombic ferroelectric phase at low
temperatures (≤300 °C) without any postdeposition annealing,
which could otherwise induce interface trap states and/or damage the
delicate MoS_(2) channel. Detailed fabrication procedures
are provided in the  section.

content.text:
The fabricated monolayer MoS_(2) FeFETs
exhibit a counterclockwise
hysteresis loop, a clear signature of ferroelectric-polarization-driven
switching behavior (b). The memory window reaches 3.6 V, corresponding to approximately
90% of the theoretical maximum value (2*E*
_(c)·*t*) derived from coercive field (*E*
_(c)) and film thickness (*t*), indicating
near-ideal utilization of the ferroelectric switching window. In addition,
the devices show a high on/off ratio exceeding 10^(7) and
a low gate leakage current of 10^(–6) A cm^(–2) (Figure S2). These representative results
demonstrate that our ferroelectric gate stacks, combined with careful
interface engineering, enable high-performance 2D FeFET operation.

To verify the ferroelectricity of as-deposited HZO, piezoresponse
force microscopy (PFM) measurements were performed on the HZO film
grown on a Y_(2)O_(3)/SiO_(2)/*p*-Si substrate (c). The phase image clearly reveals stable up- and down-polarized
domains with a phase contrast of ∼190°, indicating reliable
polarization switching. This behavior is further corroborated by characteristic
butterfly-shaped dielectric hysteresis observed over a broad frequency
range (10 kHz to 1 MHz; Figure S3). Consistently,
positive-up–negative-down (PUND) measurements using the metal–ferroelectric–insulator–metal
(MFIM) capacitor structure show well-defined *J*–*E* and *P*–*E* hysteresis
loops at 2 kHz (d), demonstrating robust remanent polarization and reproducible switching
behavior. Furthermore, independently fabricated MFIM capacitors exhibit
highly consistent *P*–*E* hysteresis
characteristics (Figure S4), confirming
minimal device-to-device variation in the ferroelectric response of
the HZO/Y_(2)O_(3) stack.

For further structural
analysis, grazing incidence X-ray diffraction
(GI-XRD) measurements (e) confirm the crystallographic phases of HZO films deposited
on the Y_(2)O_(3)/MoS_(2) stack. Prominent
diffraction peaks around 30–31°, corresponding to the
orthorhombic (111) and tetragonal (011) orientations, are clearly
observed, while no peaks associated with the monoclinic phase are
detected. This indicates that the ferroelectric orthorhombic phase
is partially stabilized in the as-deposited HZO films, effectively
suppressing the nonferroelectric monoclinic phase. The comparable
phase composition observed in both reference and MoS_(2) samples
further confirms that the presence of MoS_(2) does not interfere
with the desired crystallization behavior.
Ferroelectric Gate Stack Integration Enabled by a Y_(2)O_(3) Interfacial Layer

To enable reliable ferroelectric
integration directly onto the 2D channel, an ultrathin Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer plays critical dual roles: it acts
as a nucleation-promoting seed for HZO and simultaneously protects
the MoS_(2) surface from ALD-induced damage. A subnanometer-thick
metallic yttrium (Y) layer was deposited and spontaneously oxidized
under ambient conditions, forming Y_(2)O_(3) due to
its high oxygen reactivity. This room-temperature process minimizes
the thermal stress and prevents undesired chemical reactions at the
MoS_(2) interface.

The morphological uniformity of the
oxidized Y_(2)O_(3) seed layer was characterized by
atomic force microscopy (AFM). The root-mean-square surface roughness
of the Y_(2)O_(3)/MoS_(2) surface remains
as low as 0.17 nm (a), comparable to that of pristine MoS_(2), indicating
conformal coverage without inducing mechanical damage to the 2D surface.
The corresponding height distribution curves further support the preservation
of the underlying MoS_(2) morphology after Y_(2)O_(3) formation­(b).

content.text:
To assess possible structural and chemical damage,
Raman spectroscopy
was performed before and after seed layer formation. The E^(1)
_(2g) and A^(1)
_(g) phonon modes of MoS_(2) remain clearly identifiable with negligible shifts in peak
positions and intensity ratios (c), suggesting the Y_(2)O_(3) seeding
process does not introduce significant structural disorder. Corroborating
this observation, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirms
the chemical integrity of the interface. Specifically, the S 2p core-level
spectrum remains well-preserved without noticeable spectral broadening
or binding energy shifts, indicating that the outermost sulfur atoms
did not undergo significant chemical reactions during the seed layer
formation (Figure S5). Further, photoluminescence
(PL) spectra reveal a dominant A-exciton peak at ∼1.84 eV with
a preserved spectral line shape (Figure S6). While a slight decrease in PL intensity is observed, it may be
attributed to the dielectric screening by the high-κ overlayer
rather than any process-induced damage.

Complementary transfer
characteristics measured from the same device
using a 90 nm SiO_(2) back-gate further verify the preservation
of electronic performance (d). The key device parameters extracted from the bidirectional
transfer characteristics, including the on-state current, field-effect
mobility, and subthreshold swing, remain essentially unchanged before
and after Y_(2)O_(3) deposition (Figure S7). Consistent results are obtained from additional
MoS_(2) FETs with channel lengths ranging from 200 to 800
nm, measured at *V*
_(DS) = 0.1 V, further confirming
that the ultrathin Y_(2)O_(3) seed layer does not
appreciably degrade channel transport (Figure S8).

After subsequent HZO ALD, devices incorporating
the Y_(2)O_(3) seed layer exhibit well-preserved transport
characteristics
with substantially suppressed hysteresis, whereas devices without
Y_(2)O_(3) show pronounced back-gate hysteresis and
severely degraded field-effect mobility and a near-complete loss of
top-gate electrostatic control (Figure S9). The hysteresis-associated effective trap density is reduced by
approximately 90.5% in the presence of the Y_(2)O_(3) seed layer (Figure S10), supporting its
role in suppressing ALD-induced interfacial and near-interfacial trap
formation.

Collectively, these results demonstrate that the
ultrathin Y_(2)O_(3) layer effectively preserves the
structural,
chemical, and electrical integrity of the MoS_(2) channel
during HZO deposition while maintaining the efficient electrostatic
coupling required for high-performance FeFET operation. Furthermore,
ferroelectric characterization of HZO films with different Y_(2)O_(3) thicknesses (Figure S11)
confirms that maintaining the interfacial layer in the subnanometer
regime is essential for preserving the ferroelectric response of HZO,
with a nominal Y thickness of 0.3 nm providing the optimal balance
between effective MoS_(2) surface protection and efficient
ferroelectric gate coupling.

Following the ALD process, the
cross-sectional structure of the
full HZO/Y_(2)O_(3)/MoS_(2) gate stack was
analyzed using high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission
electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM). Fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis
of the HZO layer on MoS_(2) reveals diffraction spots corresponding
to the orthorhombic phase along the [001] zone axis (e), indicating successful ferroelectric
phase formation at low temperature, in agreement with GI-XRD analysis.
A well-defined interface with a preserved vdW gap of ∼3.3 Å
is clearly observed between the crystallized HZO and the underlying
MoS_(2) (f), suggesting minimal disruption at the interface during HZO deposition.
Note that a multilayer MoS_(2) was intentionally used for
cross-sectional TEM analyses to reduce surface roughness and enhance
image contrast. Importantly, the structural integrity is also maintained
even in the monolayer MoS_(2) channel, as confirmed by supporting
STEM imaging (Figure S11a). This supports
that the findings from multilayer observations are representative
of the monolayer devices used for all electrical measurements in this
study.

Elemental mapping by scanning transmission electron microscopy–energy
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM–EDS) further reveals a
vertically resolved composition profile across the gate stack. Sharp
elemental boundaries are observed between the channel (Mo) and dielectric
layers (Hf and Zr), with a spatially localized Y distribution near
the interface. Although the Y signal is relatively weak due to the
ultrathin nature of the interfacial layer, it remains clearly detectable,
supporting its effective role as a seed layer (g).
Electrical Performance of HZO-Top-Gated MoS_(2) FeFETs

To systematically analyze the characteristics of the HZO-top-gated
MoS_(2) FeFET fabricated through this integration scheme,
the transfer characteristics (*I*
_(DS)–*V*
_(TG) curves) were measured under various top-gate
voltage (*V*
_(TG)) sweep ranges from ±1
V to ±3.5 V. All transfer curves, plotted on a semilogarithmic
scale, exhibit clear counterclockwise hysteresis loops, indicative
of ferroelectric-polarization-driven switching behavior (a). The consistent
shape and direction of the hysteresis across all *V*
_(TG) sweep amplitudes further verify robust polarization
reversal in the HZO layer. Furthermore, the linear *I*
_(DS)–*V*
_(DS) characteristics
at various back-gate (*V*
_(BG)) and top-gate
(*V*
_(TG)) voltages confirm the formation of
Ohmic contacts between the MoS_(2) channel and source/drain
electrodes and effective electrostatic modulation by both the global
back gate and the HZO/Y_(2)O_(3) top-gate stack (a inset and Figure S12).

content.text:
To quantify the memory window (MW), the values
are extracted from
the threshold voltage difference between the forward and reverse sweeps
in the linear-scale transfer curves using linear extrapolation (b). As the sweep
range increases from ±1 V to ±3.5 V, the MWs widen proportionally.
A linear relationship is observed between the sweep range and the
MW, with a slope of ∼1.1 (inset of b), indicating proportional ferroelectric
switching behavior. This relatively large MW-to-sweep-range ratio
implies efficient electrostatic coupling through the gate stack into
the HZO layer, enabling effective polarization switching. Taken together,
these results confirm that the observed hysteresis originates from
intrinsic ferroelectric polarization reversal rather than extrinsic
effects such as charge trapping or interface state modulation.

To benchmark the performance of the monolayer MoS_(2) FeFET,
we compared the normalized MW (V nm^(–1)) and on-state
sheet conductance (μS) with those of previously reported 2D-channel
FeFETs using various ferroelectric materials (c). Since each study employed different ferroelectric
layer thicknesses, device geometries (e.g., channel width and length),
and drain bias conditions, these two parameters serve as geometry-
and bias-independent performance metrics for fair comparison. Our
monolayer MoS_(2) device demonstrates an on-state sheet conductance
of 118 μS and a normalized memory window of 0.31 V nm^(–1), which collectively represent state-of-the-art performance among
2D-channel FeFETs.
,,,−







 This highlights the effectiveness of the proposed integration scheme
and interface engineering strategy for BEOL-compatible FeFETs.

To further evaluate the reliability of devices, we performed a
series of tests, including cyclic transfer sweeps, endurance, and
retention measurements. As a first step, the device demonstrates robust
and stable ferroelectric switching behavior, under repeated DC *V*
_(TG) sweeps up to ±3.5 V, showing negligible
variation in MW and subthreshold characteristics across multiple consecutive
transfer measurements (d). It also maintains stable switching during repeated program/erase
operations using ±5 V, 1 ms *V*
_(TG) pulses
up to 10^(5) cycles, with minimal degradation in the current
levels between the high- and low-resistance states (HRS and LRS) (e). Consistently,
the extracted MW remains nearly constant at approximately 2.1–2.2
V throughout the endurance measurement (Figure S13), confirming stable switching over the tested cycling range.
Finally, the retention characteristics of HRS and LRS, initialized
by applying ±3.5 V, 1 s *V*
_(TG) pulses,
are evaluated over time (f). The two states remain clearly distinguishable for
over 10^(4) s under the present measurement conditions. However,
gradual reduction in the read margin is observed, indicating that
further improvement is required to achieve embedded-NVM-level retention.
We attribute this limitation primarily to the relatively modest switchable
polarization of the annealing-free HZO film. Although the ultrathin
Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer and atomically thin MoS_(2) channel enable efficient electrostatic coupling and a large
initial MW, further optimization of the annealing-free HZO ferroelectric
properties will be required to improve long-term retention.
Benchmarking of MoS_(2) FeFETs

To assess the
competitiveness of our device within the broader landscape of ferroelectric-based
device technologies, we conducted a comprehensive benchmarking analysis
that includes various FeFETs based on 2D materials, oxide semiconductors,
and silicon channels while explicitly excluding MFMIS-based architectures. a presents the normalized
MW as a function of operation voltage, comparing hafnia-based (green),
AlScN-based (blue), and our HZO-based (red) FeFETs across both top-gated
and bottom-gated architectures.

content.text:
Our monolayer MoS_(2) device consistently
demonstrates
a large normalized MW at low operation voltages, clearly outperforming
previously reported 2D-channel FeFETs and even rivaling or surpassing
silicon-based counterparts. Notably, the operation voltage achieved
here satisfies the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS)
target for low-voltage FeFETs (≤3 V), underscoring both CMOS
compatibility and energy efficiency of our integration approach. This
superior performance arises from the synergistic combination of an
atomically thin MoS_(2) channel, an ultrathin, high-κ
Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer, and a low-temperature-crystallized
HZO film. Together, these components enable efficient electrostatic
coupling, suppress interfacial trap formation, and facilitate robust
ferroelectric switching, even at reduced voltages.

In terms
of BEOL process compatibility, furthermore, our device
offers a remarkable advantage; it achieves the highest reported MW-to-maximum
voltage (MW/*V*
_(MAX)) ratio to date among
all BEOL-compatible FeFETs. Notably, this exceptional performance
is achieved despite the entire device fabrication process being conducted
below 300 °C, well within the industry-standard thermal budget
of 400 °C (b).
,,,,,,
 This benchmarking analysis highlights
the strong promise of our integration strategy for next-generation
ferroelectric-based devices and their monolithic 3D integration, by
combining excellent normalized performance with full compliance to
BEOL and IRDS requirements.
Conclusions

We demonstrated a BEOL-compatible 2D FeFET
by integrating an annealing-free
HZO ferroelectric layer on monolayer MoS_(2), enabled by an
ultrathin high-κ Y_(2)O_(3) interfacial layer
that facilitates conformal ALD. The resulting device exhibits a large
memory window of 3.6 V at ±3.5 V, corresponding to ∼90%
of the theoretical maximum, together with a high on/off ratio of 10^(7), retention exceeding 10^(4) s, and endurance over
10^(5) cycles. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms our monolayer
MoS_(2) device not only outperforms previously reported FeFETs
based on diverse channel materials in normalized performance metrics
but also satisfies the IRDS low-voltage operation guideline despite
being fabricated entirely within BEOL thermal constraints. These results
highlight the potential of our integration strategy for next-generation
low-power memory and logic-in-memory devices, particularly in monolithic
3D integration platforms.
Methods
Device Fabrication

Devices were fabricated on *p*-Si substrates with a 90 nm SiO_(2) dielectric
layer. To ensure a clean channel interface, bottom contact electrodes
were defined prior to channel transfer. Electron-beam lithography
(EBL) was performed using a bilayer polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
resist stack (495 K A4 and 950 K C4, MicroChem), spin-coated at 4000
rpm for 45 s and baked at 180 °C for 2 min each. After e-beam
exposure, the resist was developed in a 1:3 mixture of methyl isobutyl
ketone (MIBK) and isopropanol (IPA) for 3 min and rinsed in IPA for
1 min to stop development. Subsequently, Ti/Au (2/15 nm) bottom electrodes
were deposited by electron-beam evaporation at a rate of 1 Å
s^(–1), followed by lift-off in acetone overnight with
mild sonication. As the channel material, monolayer single-crystalline
MoS_(2) flakes (HQ Graphene) were mechanically exfoliated
onto 285 nm SiO_(2)/*p*-Si substrates that
had been cleaned by O_(2) plasma (100 W, 10 min; FemtoSci.)
prior to exfoliation. Selected flakes were picked up using a conventional
wet-transfer method with a polypropylene carbonate (PPC) layer supported
on a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp and were precisely aligned
onto the prepatterned bottom electrodes using a micromanipulator-equipped
probe station. The stack was then brought into contact at 60 °C
for 1 min to facilitate release of the MoS_(2). The residual
PPC layer was removed by sequential soaking in acetone at 60 °C
for 1 h followed by *N*-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP)
at 80 °C for at least 2 h. A sub-nm-thick Y layer was deposited
by thermal evaporation at a slow rate of 0.05–0.1 Å s^(–1) to ensure smooth morphology and precise thickness
control. No additional oxidation was performed. The inherently high
reactivity of Y led to its spontaneous oxidation upon exposure to
ambient air. The HZO was then deposited by ALD at 300 °C using
alternating cycles of tetrakis­(ethylmethylamino)­zirconium
(TEMA-Zr) and tetrakis­(ethylmethylamino)­hafnium (TEMA-Hf),
with H_(2)O as the reactant. No postdeposition annealing was
conducted. Top-gate electrodes were patterned using the same EBL process
described above. Tungsten (W, 30 nm) was deposited by room-temperature
DC sputtering, followed by lift-off in acetone at room temperature
for more than 1 h with mild sonication.
Electrical Measurements

All electrical measurements
were carried out under ambient conditions (room temperature and atmospheric
pressure). DC current–voltage (*I*–*V*) characteristics of the FeFETs were measured using a Keysight
E5270B precision measurement system. For pulsed measurements of both
FeFETs and metal–ferroelectric–insulator–metal
(MFIM) capacitor structures, a Keithley 4200A semiconductor parameter
analyzer equipped with a waveform generator/fast measurement unit
(WGFMU) was employed.
Ferroelectric Characterization

To assess the ferroelectric
behavior of HZO films without thermal annealing, CR-PFM was performed.
Measurements were conducted on a Park Systems NX10 atomic force microscope
equipped with a high-frequency actuation module (NOST) and a conductive
Cr/Pt-coated probe (ElectriMulti75-G; nominal tip radius ∼25
nm). A high-frequency AC voltage (>100 kHz) was applied to the
AFM
tip to excite mechanical vibrations near its contact resonance, and
the out-of-plane cantilever motion was detected using an optical beam
deflection system. The structural characteristics of the annealing-free
HZO films were examined by GI-XRD (X’Pert PRO, PANalytical)
using a Cu Kα source (λ = 1.5406 Å) and a point detector
at a fixed incidence angle of ∼0.5°, with a scan rate
of 1° min^(–1) in 2θ.
Optical Spectroscopy

Raman and PL measurements were
performed using a micro-optical setup comprising a 532 nm continuous-wave
laser (power: 120 μW) and a grating monochromator (Andor 303i).
A 300 grooves mm^(–1) grating was used for PL spectroscopy
to capture a broad emission range, while Raman spectra were recorded
with a high-resolution 1800 grooves mm^(–1) grating
to accurately resolve the distinct vibrational modes.
Surface Characterization

AFM was employed primarily
to quantify the surface roughness of MoS_(2) channels before
and after Y_(2)O_(3) deposition, with additional thickness
profiling to verify the monolayer nature of MoS_(2). Measurements
were performed on an NX10 system (Park Systems) using PPP-NCHR silicon
cantilevers (Nanosensors) operated in noncontact mode. Topography
data were preprocessed by first-order plane leveling and line-by-line
flattening prior to analysis.
TEM Imaging and Analysis

Cross-sectional TEM specimens
were prepared by focused ion beam (FIB) milling using a Helios Nanolab
600 system (FEI). The crystallinity and elemental distribution of
the HZO films were examined by HAADF-STEM and STEM-EDS using a Titan
80-300 microscope (FEI) operated at an accelerating voltage of 300
kV in STEM mode.
